rw: Forming is the first stage, where members are polite, cautious and uncertain about roles and expectations while they get to know each other, which matches this new team exactly.

ww.Storming: Storming is the stage of open disagreement and power struggles, but this team is polite and cautious rather than arguing, so this stage does not fit the situation described.
ww.Norming: Norming comes after members have settled their roles and built shared rules and trust, but this team is still unsure of its roles, so it has not reached that point.
ww.Performing: Performing describes a mature team working smoothly with clear roles and high output, which is the opposite of a team that is still unsure what each person should do.

rw: Storming is the stage where members compete over leadership and challenge how work should be done, so open arguments about who leads and the method are the typical sign of it.

ww.Adjourning: Adjourning is the final stage when the work ends and the team disbands, but this team is still active and arguing over leadership, so it has not reached an ending.
ww.Norming: Norming is when members resolve their differences and agree on roles and working rules, but this team is still fighting about who leads, so that agreement has not happened yet.
ww.Forming: Forming is the polite, uncertain first stage where members avoid conflict, but this team is openly arguing about leadership and methods, which is far beyond that cautious start.

rw: Adjourning is the last stage, when the project is complete and members separate to new assignments, which is exactly what happens when a team finishes its project and disperses.

ww.Storming: Storming involves conflict over roles and leadership while the team is still working together, but this team has completed its project and is disbanding, so that stage is long past.
ww.Forming: Forming is the beginning stage when people first meet and learn their roles, but this team is finishing and separating, which is the end of its life, not the start.
ww.Norming: Norming is the middle stage where members settle into agreed roles and working habits, but this team has already completed its work and is breaking up, so it is past that stage.

rw: Marketing, finance and operations each bring different expertise and viewpoints, so the team can spot problems and generate solutions that a single-department group would miss, which is the main benefit of cross-functional teams.

ww.Less communication flow: Mixing departments usually makes communication more complex and demands more coordination, not less, and reduced communication would hurt the team, so this cannot be called a benefit of the structure.
ww.Everyone thinks alike: People from different functions bring different backgrounds and priorities, so they rarely think alike, and uniform thinking would actually weaken the team, so this is not a benefit.
ww.Fewer ideas and views: Combining three departments adds knowledge and perspectives rather than removing them, so the team should produce more ideas, not fewer, which makes this option the reverse of the true benefit.

rw: Shared tools let members see the same information at any hour, and agreed meeting times that rotate fairly respect each zone, so this combination best supports a team spread across time zones.

ww.Meetings at random hours of the day or n: Random meeting hours would force people in some time zones to join in the middle of the night, hurting rest and attendance, so this makes coordination worse rather than better for a spread team.
ww.Different tools for each person, with no: Separate tools with no sharing would leave information scattered and unavailable to others, which creates confusion and delays that are even worse when members cannot meet at the same hour.
ww.No communication at all between the memb: Without any communication the members cannot coordinate tasks, share progress or solve problems, and distance already makes teamwork harder, so cutting contact would cause the team to fail outright.

rw: Ground rules for taking turns set clear, fair expectations for everyone, address the interruptions without attacking the person, and let all members be heard, making this the constructive team response.

ww.Ban the member from meetings so others c: Banning the member from meetings excludes a team member, damages trust and removes their useful input, and it punishes the person rather than fixing the behavior with a fair shared rule.
ww.Interrupt back at the member each time: Interrupting back copies the bad behavior, escalates tension and makes meetings more chaotic, so it teaches nothing and leaves the original problem unsolved while adding a new one.
ww.Let the member dominate every meeting: Letting one member dominate every meeting silences the others and wastes their ideas, so the team loses balanced participation and the interruptions continue without any consequence at all.

rw: Synergy means the team's combined effort produces results greater than the sum of what the members could achieve separately, so two plus two exceeds four through cooperation and shared skills.

ww.Each person working alone on a separate: Working alone on separate tasks with no shared goals is the absence of teamwork, so it cannot produce the extra value that defines synergy, which depends on members combining their efforts.
ww.Lower output from the team as members wo: Lower output as members work less hard describes social loafing, which is a team problem, while synergy means the group achieves more, not less, than expected from the people involved.
ww.Conflict between members that slows the: Conflict that slows the whole team is a failure of teamwork, not synergy, because synergy describes cooperation that raises results above what the individuals could produce working alone.

rw: Consensus is a decision method where every member must agree before the team proceeds, so the requirement that everyone agree matches the definition of consensus exactly.

ww.Autocracy: Autocracy means one person decides alone without needing others to agree, which is the opposite of a decision that requires everyone to agree before the team moves forward.
ww.Majority rule: Majority rule only needs more than half of the members to agree, so some people can disagree and the decision still passes, which does not match a rule needing everyone's agreement.
ww.Random choice: Random choice picks an outcome by chance, such as a coin flip, without regard to anyone's agreement, so it has nothing to do with requiring every member to approve.

rw: Majority rule means the option with the most votes wins, even if some members disagree, so a team that votes and follows the highest count is using exactly this method.

ww.Consensus: Consensus needs every member to agree before the team proceeds, but here the most votes wins and some people may disagree, so full agreement is not required.
ww.Compromise: Compromise means each side gives up something to meet in the middle, but a vote simply counts support for options, and the winner takes the result with no one giving ground.
ww.Autocracy: Autocracy places the decision in one person's hands, but here the whole team votes and the count decides, so the group, not a single leader, makes the choice.

rw: Crediting the team for a win shows respect for everyone's contribution, which raises morale and builds trust in the leader, and that makes members willing to keep cooperating and working hard.

ww.Wastes time and money: Giving credit costs nothing and takes only a moment, so it does not waste time or money, and it tends to improve effort and cooperation that benefit the organization overall.
ww.Creates open conflict: Sharing credit recognizes everyone's contribution, which lowers resentment and rivalry, so it does not create open conflict and is more likely to strengthen the relationships among team members.
ww.Reduces team motivation: Recognition normally increases motivation because members feel valued, so crediting the team would raise rather than reduce motivation, and the reverse would happen only if leaders took all the credit.

rw: Short paragraphs, bullet points and a clear subject line separate each request so the reader can see and act on every one quickly, which directly fixes the problem of buried requests.

ww.Remove the subject line and write one lo: Removing the subject line and using one long paragraph makes the email harder to scan and the separate requests easy to miss, which makes it less clear, not more.
ww.Use bigger words and longer sentences th: Bigger words and longer sentences make the message harder to read and understand, so the requests become even more confusing instead of being easier for the reader to follow.
ww.Add more unrelated information to give a: Adding unrelated information buries the requests under extra details and distracts the reader from the main points, so the email becomes longer and less clear rather than clearer.

rw: Feedback is the receiver's response that lets the sender check understanding, and without it the sender could not detect or correct the customer's misunderstanding, so it is the missing element.

ww.A message sent by the sender here: The sender did send a message to the customer, otherwise there would be nothing to misunderstand, so a sent message was not missing and this does not explain the failure.
ww.A channel used to send messages: A channel was clearly used, since the message reached the customer, so the channel was present, and its presence does not explain why the customer misunderstood the meaning of the message.
ww.A sender who writes the message: A sender wrote the message, so a sender existed in this process, and the misunderstanding came after the message was received, not from the lack of a sender.

rw: Jargon is specialized language that a general audience does not know, so it blocks understanding and becomes a barrier, which is the problem when a speaker uses technical terms with non-experts.

ww.A clear message that the audience grasps: A clear message the audience grasps at once is a sign of effective communication, not a barrier, so it cannot describe the problem that jargon creates for a general audience.
ww.Short sentences that are easy for anyone: Short, easy sentences help communication, while the problem here is unfamiliar technical vocabulary, so sentence length does not describe the barrier that jargon creates for the listeners.
ww.Too much eye contact with the listeners: Eye contact normally helps a speaker connect with listeners, and it has nothing to do with the confusion caused by technical terms that the audience does not understand.

rw: A written memo or email provides a detailed, permanent record that reaches every employee, and a follow-up meeting allows questions, so it suits a formal policy change affecting everyone.

ww.A text message to a few staff from a per: A text from a personal phone to a few staff cannot reach everyone, lacks a formal record and detail, and is unsuited to a policy that affects all employees.
ww.A quick hallway comment made in passing: A hallway comment in passing is informal, reaches almost no one and leaves no record, so it cannot convey a detailed formal policy change to the entire workforce reliably.
ww.A rumor passed along by word of mouth am: A rumor spread by word of mouth distorts the details, reaches people unevenly and is not official, so it is a poor way to announce a formal policy.

rw: A private face-to-face conversation allows tact, tone and body language, lets the employee respond immediately and protects privacy, making it the best channel for delicate performance feedback.

ww.A group email sent to the whole firm: A group email to the whole firm exposes a sensitive matter to people who should not see it, which embarrasses the employee and makes the feedback less likely to be accepted.
ww.A social media post seen by many: A social media post is public, impersonal and seen by many, so it would embarrass the employee and could damage the relationship, which makes it unsuitable for sensitive feedback.
ww.A text message sent late at night: A late-night text lacks tone and context, can be misread, and does not allow a real discussion, so it is a risky way to deliver delicate feedback about performance.

rw: Words say excited while the floor-gazing and crossed arms suggest discomfort or disinterest, so the audience gets contradictory signals, and people tend to trust the nonverbal message over the spoken one.

ww.Honesty and openness shown through the s: Honesty and openness would be shown by open posture and eye contact, but looking at the floor with crossed arms signals the opposite, so the audience would not perceive these qualities.
ww.A clear, consistent message as the words: The words and body language disagree, since excitement does not look like crossed arms and a downward gaze, so the audience would not see a consistent message, which makes this option false.
ww.Great enthusiasm that the whole audience: Great enthusiasm usually appears through energy, eye contact and open gestures, none of which are present, so the audience is unlikely to see enthusiasm in a speaker who looks away.

rw: A you attitude puts the reader first by stressing what they need and how they will benefit, which makes the message more relevant and persuasive, and that is what the term means.

ww.Avoid mentioning the reader at any point: A you attitude is about directing the message toward the reader, so avoiding any mention of the reader goes against the approach and would make the writing seem cold and self-centered.
ww.Use the word 'you' in every sentence: Counting the word you in every sentence is a mechanical trick that misses the point, as the attitude concerns focusing on the reader's needs and benefits, not on repeating a particular word.
ww.Focus on yourself and the firm in each l: Focusing on yourself and the firm is the opposite of a you attitude, which places the reader's interests first, so it would produce writing that seems self-centered and less persuasive.

rw: A hostile tone makes readers feel attacked, so they are likely to become defensive and resist the message even when the facts are correct, and that damages the communication.

ww.The facts become false at once: Tone does not change whether facts are true or false, so correct facts remain accurate even when worded harshly, and this option confuses the quality of the content with its delivery.
ww.The message is much clearer to all: Hostile wording adds emotional noise that distracts from the content, so the message becomes less clear and less well received, which is the reverse of becoming much clearer to everyone.
ww.The reader will always agree with it: Readers who feel attacked tend to resist and push back, so a hostile tone makes agreement less likely, and saying the reader will always agree ignores that reaction and overstates the case.

rw: Stating the purpose and why it matters to the audience gives listeners a reason to pay attention and a clear framework, which makes it a strong, widely recommended way to open.

ww.Read the slides word for word to the aud: Reading the slides word for word is dull, adds nothing the audience cannot read for themselves and weakens engagement, so it is a poor way to open a presentation.
ww.Apologize for being nervous before you e: Apologizing for nervousness draws attention to weakness, lowers the audience's confidence in the speaker and does not help them understand the topic, so it is a weak opening.
ww.Start with unrelated jokes only, so the: Jokes unrelated to the topic may amuse briefly but do not tell the audience why they are there, and using only jokes leaves the purpose unclear, so this is a weak opening.

rw: Moving to table sets the pending motion aside to be taken up at a later time, which is a form of postponing it without a decision, so this describes the term correctly.

ww.Rejecting it: Rejecting a motion is done by voting it down, not by tabling it, and a tabled motion is set aside rather than defeated, so this confuses tabling with a negative vote.
ww.Amending it: Amending a motion changes its wording through a motion to amend, while tabling sets the motion aside without changing it, so the two are different procedures and this answer is wrong.
ww.Approving it: Approving a motion requires a vote in favor, which is separate from tabling, because a tabled motion has not been decided and nothing has been approved or adopted yet.

rw: A motion to amend is the procedure for changing the wording of a pending motion, so a member who wants different wording should move to amend, and this is the correct step.

ww.Call the question: Calling the question asks to end debate and vote right away, which does not change the wording of a motion, so it is not the correct step for revising the motion.
ww.Move to table: Moving to table sets a motion aside for later and leaves the wording exactly as it is, so it does not change the language of the motion as the member wants.
ww.Move to adjourn: Moving to adjourn proposes ending the whole meeting and has nothing to do with editing a motion, so it would stop business rather than change the wording of the motion.

rw: Calling the question asks the group to stop debating and vote on the pending matter immediately, so ending debate and bringing the matter to a vote is its exact effect.

ww.Adjourns the meeting at once for the day: Adjourning the meeting is done through a separate motion to adjourn, while calling the question concerns the matter under discussion, so ending the whole meeting is the wrong effect for it.
ww.Cancels the vote and the motion on the f: Calling the question moves toward a vote rather than canceling one, and it does not remove the motion, so cancelling the vote and the motion is the reverse of its effect.
ww.Starts debate on the matter before the c: Debate starts when a motion is made and seconded, whereas calling the question is used later to stop discussion, so starting debate is the opposite of what the call does.

rw: Upward communication flows from lower levels to higher ones, so an employee sending a progress report to a manager moves information up the hierarchy, making this a clear example.

ww.A manager giving orders to a team about: A manager giving orders to a team sends information down the hierarchy to subordinates, which is downward communication, so it is not an example of upward communication.
ww.A memo from the CEO to all of the staff: A memo from the CEO to all staff moves from the top of the organization down to employees, which is downward communication, so it is not upward.
ww.A friend chatting at lunch about the wee: A chat between friends at lunch about weekend plans is personal social talk and not a work message moving up the chain of command, so it is not upward communication.

rw: Downward communication flows from higher levels to lower ones, so a manager handing out instructions to workers at the start of a shift is a standard example of it.

ww.Grapevine communication: The grapevine is the informal network through which gossip and rumors spread, whereas handing out official instructions at the start of a shift is a formal, planned message.
ww.Upward communication: Upward communication flows from employees to managers, but here the manager is sending instructions to workers, so the direction is reversed and this answer does not describe the situation.
ww.Lateral communication: Lateral communication happens between people at the same level, but a manager instructing workers is communicating with those below, so it is not lateral communication in this case.

rw: Department heads are peers at the same level, and information exchanged between peers is lateral or horizontal communication, so it matches this situation exactly.

ww.Grapevine communication among staff: The grapevine is informal and unofficial, often carrying gossip, while two department heads sharing project information are conducting official business, so it does not fit the grapevine.
ww.Downward communication from managers: Downward communication goes from managers to their subordinates, but two department heads are at the same level, so neither is sending information down to the other.
ww.Upward communication to the boss: Upward communication goes from subordinates to a boss, but the two department heads are peers rather than one reporting to the other, so the flow is not upward.

rw: Each person gives up part of what they wanted by sharing the room at different times, and meeting in the middle with mutual concessions is compromise, so it fits.

ww.Accommodation: Accommodation means one person simply gives in and lets the other have their way, but here both parties adjust and share the room, so neither one fully yields.
ww.Competition: Competition means one side tries to win at the other's expense, but these employees agreed on a shared schedule, so neither one imposed their wishes on the other.
ww.Avoidance: Avoidance means ignoring or withdrawing from the conflict, but these employees addressed the issue directly and reached an agreement on the room, so the conflict was not avoided.

rw: Both parties gained something they wanted, the buyer a lower price and the seller a longer contract, so each came out ahead and the outcome is win-win.

ww.No deal: A deal was reached because both sides agreed on terms, so calling it no deal contradicts the facts of the scenario, where the buyer and the seller reached an agreement.
ww.Lose-lose: Lose-lose means both sides end up worse off, but here both receive something they wanted, a lower price and a longer contract, so neither party loses.
ww.Win-lose: Win-lose means one side gains at the other's expense, but both the buyer and the seller got what they wanted, so the result is not a one-sided win.

rw: Anchoring sets an initial, often extreme figure that shapes the range for the rest of the talks, so opening with an extreme demand to set that range is exactly this tactic.

ww.Stalling: Stalling means delaying the talks to gain time or pressure, but opening with an extreme demand sets the range of the discussion rather than delaying it, so this is not the tactic.
ww.Framing: Framing means presenting an issue in a particular way or context, whereas this tactic sets a starting figure that influences the range of the talks, which is a different tactic.
ww.Mirroring: Mirroring means copying the other person's words or body language to build rapport, which has nothing to do with opening with an extreme demand to set the range.

rw: In mediation a neutral third party helps the disputants communicate and reach their own agreement without imposing a decision, which is what happens with these two coworkers.

ww.Arbitration: Arbitration has the neutral party hear both sides and issue a binding decision, but here the coworkers reach their own agreement, so the third party is not deciding the outcome.
ww.Litigation: Litigation is a legal dispute settled in court by a judge, which is a formal process that does not match a neutral helper guiding coworkers to their own agreement.
ww.Avoidance: Avoidance means staying away from the conflict, but here a neutral third party actively helps resolve it, so the dispute is being addressed rather than ignored.

rw: Arbitration has a neutral third party hear both sides and then issue a decision that is binding, so the parties must accept it, which matches the description exactly.

ww.Compromise: Compromise is when the parties themselves each give something up, but here a neutral third party imposes the decision, so the parties are not reaching a middle ground by themselves.
ww.Mediation: In mediation the neutral party only helps the sides reach their own agreement and does not issue a binding decision, so it differs from the described process where a decision is imposed.
ww.Collaboration: Collaboration is when the parties work together to find a joint solution themselves, but here an outsider decides and the decision binds the parties, so it does not fit.

rw: An interest is the underlying need or reason behind a demand, and needing to finish before school pickup explains why, leaving room for flexible solutions, so this statement shows an interest.

ww.'I will only leave at 4 p.m. and that is: Leaving at 4 p.m. as a position is a fixed demand that states what the person will do without explaining the reason behind it, so it is a position, not an interest.
ww.'No, that is not possible and I will not: Refusing to discuss the matter is a rigid stance that shuts down the talks and gives no underlying reason, so it is a position and does not reveal any interest.
ww.'That is my final offer and I will not c: A final offer that will not change is a fixed position that stops the negotiation and shares no underlying need, so it is not an interest.

rw: Avoiding means withdrawing from a conflict or ignoring it in the hope it will go away, which is exactly what this team member does, so this is the avoiding style.

ww.Compromise: Compromise involves both sides discussing and giving up something, but this member avoids the disagreement entirely and does not engage, so there is no give and take at all.
ww.Teaming up: Teaming up is not a recognized conflict style, and the member is not working with anyone to resolve the issue but is avoiding the discussion in the hope it ends.
ww.Competing: Competing means pushing hard to win your own position, while this member withdraws and avoids the disagreement, so the behavior is the opposite of competing and does not match.

rw: Collaborating means working together with all parties to find a solution that fully meets everyone's needs, so the manager working with both sides toward that goal fits this style.

ww.Competing: Competing means pushing for your own interests and trying to win, but this manager works with both parties to meet everyone's needs, which is cooperative rather than competitive.
ww.Avoidance: Avoidance means ignoring or withdrawing from the conflict, but this manager actively engages both parties and seeks a solution, so the behavior is the reverse of avoidance.
ww.Accommodating: Accommodating means giving in to the other side's wishes, but here the manager seeks a solution meeting everyone's needs, so no one simply yields to the other.

rw: Accommodating means yielding to the other person's demands to preserve the relationship or keep the peace, which describes someone who gives in for those reasons, so it fits.

ww.Compromising: Compromising means both sides give up something to meet in the middle, but here only one person gives in to the other's demands, so the concession is one-sided.
ww.Competing: Competing means pursuing your own goals against the other person, but this person yields to keep the peace instead of pushing, so the behavior is the opposite of competing.
ww.Collaborating: Collaborating means working with the other party to meet both sides' needs, but this person simply gives in, so no joint problem solving happens and it does not fit.

rw: A strong alternative lets her walk away without a loss, so she can insist on better terms, and that stronger fallback increases her bargaining power in the negotiation.

ww.It reduces her bargaining power: A strong alternative means she can walk away without suffering, which raises her leverage, so saying it reduces her bargaining power reverses the actual effect on her position.
ww.It has no effect on her position: An alternative to the deal strongly affects how much she can demand, because she is less dependent on the other party, so claiming no effect ignores a main source of bargaining power.
ww.It forces her to accept the terms: Having a good alternative means she does not have to accept poor terms, so it frees her from being forced to accept, which is the opposite of what this answer says.

rw: The salesperson offers a concession, a lower price, in exchange for something from the customer, a two-year commitment, and giving one thing for another is a trade-off offer.

ww.An insult to him: Offering a lower price in return for a two-year signature is a normal business proposal, not an insult, since it treats the customer respectfully and invites agreement from him.
ww.A threat to him: A threat would warn of a bad consequence if the customer refuses, but this statement offers a benefit in exchange for a commitment, so it is an incentive rather than a threat.
ww.A refusal to talk: The salesperson is offering conditions to reach a deal, so this is an active attempt to continue the talks, not a refusal to talk with the customer.

rw: Preparing, listening and staying calm let a negotiator understand both sides, make sound proposals and avoid emotional mistakes, so these behaviors are the ones most likely to produce a good agreement.

ww.Making threats to the other party: Threats create hostility and defensiveness in the other party, which makes agreement harder, so they damage the negotiation rather than help it.
ww.Interrupting the other side often: Interrupting the other side shows disrespect and prevents the negotiator from learning their needs, which harms trust and makes a good agreement less likely.
ww.Hiding all facts from the other side: Hiding all facts blocks the trust and information sharing needed to find solutions that work for both sides, so it hurts a negotiation instead of helping it.

rw: Listening shows respect, explaining the policy gives the customer a clear reason, and offering alternatives such as store credit gives a fair solution, which can keep the customer satisfied.

ww.Hang up the phone at once and leave the: Hanging up the phone abandons the customer, escalates the anger and damages the company's reputation, and it leaves the problem unresolved, so it is an unprofessional and harmful reply.
ww.Say nothing in reply and wait for the cu: Saying nothing and waiting for the customer to leave ignores the complaint, increases frustration and shows poor service, so it does not address the problem or help the customer.
ww.Argue that the customer should have read: Arguing that the customer should have read the policy blames the customer, escalates the conflict and offers no solution, so it will probably lose the customer and harm goodwill.

rw: After setting a goal, planners should develop strategies and action plans that describe how it will be reached, so this is the natural next step following the goal.

ww.Forget the goal and carry on as the firm: Forgetting the goal and carrying on as before drops the target the company has just set, so nothing would be done to increase sales, which contradicts the purpose of setting it.
ww.Hire no one and keep the same plan as in: Hiring no one and keeping the old plan changes nothing about how the company works, so there is no action to lift sales by 10 percent and the goal would be ignored.
ww.Cut all prices to zero so every customer: Cutting all prices to zero would remove revenue completely and destroy the business, so it would not raise sales results in any sensible way, even if customers took the goods.

rw: Contingency planning prepares alternative actions in case a key event such as a supplier failure occurs, so preparing a backup plan for this risk is the very definition of it.

ww.Operational planning: Operational planning covers day-to-day activities and short-term tasks, but a backup plan for a supplier failure is prepared for an unexpected problem, so it is not operational planning.
ww.Strategic planning: Strategic planning sets the company's long-term direction and major goals, but a backup plan for one supplier failing responds to a specific risk, so it is not strategic planning.
ww.Budgetary planning: Budgetary planning deals with allocating money and setting financial limits, while a backup plan for a supplier failure concerns what to do if events go wrong, so it does not fit.

rw: Opening a second location in three years is a long-range goal that sets the direction of the business, so it is an example of long-term strategic planning.

ww.Hourly staffing schedules only: Hourly staffing schedules cover very short-term operations and not a goal three years away, so this answer describes the wrong planning level for opening a second location.
ww.Daily scheduling of kitchen staff: Daily scheduling of kitchen staff is routine short-term operational planning, so it does not describe a three-year goal such as opening another restaurant.
ww.Weekly ordering of supplies: Weekly ordering of supplies is a short-term operating task repeated every week and does not describe a three-year goal of opening a new location, so it is the wrong type of planning.

rw: Increasing monthly sales by 8 percent by June 30 is specific, measurable and time-bound, and it can be achieved and relevant, so it meets the SMART criteria.

ww.Be the best company in the whole region: Being the best company in the region soon is vague, because best and soon have no measure or deadline, so it lacks the specific and measurable parts that SMART requires.
ww.Try harder to sell more of the products: Try harder to sell more has no number, no deadline and no way to tell whether it was achieved, so it fails the specific, measurable and time-bound parts of a SMART goal.
ww.Sell a lot more soon using the best meth: Sell a lot more soon using the best methods is vague, with no number, no deadline and no clear method, so it fails the SMART test for specific and measurable goals.

rw: Controlling means comparing actual results with the plan and making adjustments, and a manager who compares monthly sales to the plan and then adjusts staffing is doing exactly that.

ww.Staffing: Staffing is the function of hiring, training and placing employees, but the manager here is checking results against the plan, so the function described is monitoring, not recruiting people.
ww.Organizing: Organizing arranges resources and tasks into a structure, but this manager is measuring actual sales against targets and adjusting afterwards, which is a monitoring activity and not a structuring one.
ww.Planning: Planning sets goals and decides actions in advance, but this manager is reviewing results that already happened against an existing plan, so the activity is controlling rather than planning.

rw: Markets, costs, competitors and resources change over time, so reviewing plans regularly lets managers update them to fit the new situation and avoid acting on outdated assumptions.

ww.Plans never change once they are written: Plans do change when conditions shift, and saying they never change once written is false, which is exactly why they need to be reviewed and revised from time to time.
ww.Reviews cause failure as staff lose time: Reviews do not cause failure, because they help managers catch problems early, so claiming that staff lose time to act reverses the benefit of reviewing plans regularly.
ww.Review wastes time that staff could use: Review takes a little time but prevents wasted work on an outdated plan, so it saves effort overall, and calling it a waste ignores the value of keeping plans current.

rw: A milestone marks a key point or achievement in the project schedule, such as finishing a phase, which lets managers track progress, so this is the correct definition.

ww.A daily task for one team member to fini: A daily task for one member is a small work item and not a major marker in the schedule, so it describes an activity instead of a milestone.
ww.A staff member who works in the project: A staff member in the project team is a resource, not a point in the schedule, so it describes a person instead of a milestone in the plan.
ww.A budget item that lists a cost for the: A budget item listing a cost belongs to the project's financial plan, not to its schedule, so it does not describe a milestone, which marks progress in time.

rw: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks, and it determines the shortest possible project duration, because any delay on it delays the entire project.

ww.The balance sheet: A balance sheet reports a company's assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time, so it does not show task dependencies or the longest chain that sets a project's length.
ww.The org chart: An org chart shows reporting relationships among people in a company and says nothing about task order or the time needed to finish a project, so it does not fit.
ww.The fishbone diagram: A fishbone diagram traces the causes of a problem and does not show task dependencies or the length of a schedule, so it cannot reveal the chain that sets duration.

rw: Assessing the effect on time and cost and agreeing changes with the client before starting follows proper change control, which keeps the project realistic and the client informed and in agreement.

ww.Refuse to discuss changes of any kind an: Refusing to discuss any change ignores the client's needs and risks losing the relationship, because project plans often need to adapt, so this rigid approach is not good project management.
ww.Add the features secretly without tellin: Adding the features secretly with no change to price or schedule is dishonest and overloads the team, and it will likely cause delays, cost overruns and loss of the client's trust.
ww.Accept every request without question, s: Accepting every request without question causes scope creep, which strains the budget and schedule, because added features take time and money that the original plan did not include.

rw: A sprint is a short, time-boxed period, often two to four weeks, in which an agile team completes a planned set of work, which matches this definition exactly.

ww.A long project phase lasting years and i: A sprint is short and fixed, usually weeks, so a long phase lasting years does not describe it, and a sprint involves the project team rather than all of the staff.
ww.A race between team members to finish th: A sprint is a time-boxed period of cooperative teamwork and not a competition between members for a prize, so a race to finish tasks first is not what the word means.
ww.A meeting to assign blame for delays hel: Assigning blame is not the purpose of a sprint, which is a period of work, and a meeting held monthly by managers does not describe a sprint at all.

rw: Delaying the launch and fixing the defect protects customers and the company's reputation, because a major defect is more costly after release, so it is the responsible choice.

ww.Hide the defect from the customers: Hiding the defect from customers is dishonest, endangers them and risks legal trouble and lost trust, so it is unethical and unprofessional, whatever the pressure to meet the date.
ww.Launch anyway and hope no one notices: Launching anyway and hoping no one notices releases a flawed product to customers, which risks harm, returns, lawsuits and lost trust, so hope is not a responsible plan.
ww.Blame the testers for the defect: Blaming the testers is unfair, since they found the defect as they should, and blame does not fix the product, so it does nothing to solve the problem.

rw: A project charter formally authorizes the project, names the sponsor and states its purpose, so it gives the manager authority to start, which is its main function.

ww.Records the project's costs and the hour: Costs and hours worked are recorded in budget and time-tracking documents, not in the charter, which is prepared at the start to approve the project, so it does not record them.
ww.Evaluates staff on how well they have do: Evaluating staff performance is done through performance reviews and not through the charter, whose job is to authorize and define the project at the start, so this is incorrect.
ww.Lists tasks completed by the team with d: Listing completed tasks with dates and names belongs to progress reports or logs kept during the project, whereas a charter is created at the beginning to authorize the project.

rw: Spending 70 percent of the budget for one-third of the work projects a total near $42,000, because $14,000 times three is $42,000, so the project may exceed its $20,000 budget.

ww.The project is already finished: Only one-third of the work is done, so the project is far from finished, and a project that has used 70 percent of its budget while unfinished is not complete.
ww.The project is right on track: Spending $14,000 of $20,000, which is 70 percent, for one-third of the work, is well ahead of progress, so the project is not on track in terms of cost.
ww.The project is well under budget: Being under budget would require spending less than the work done warrants, yet 70 percent of the money has gone to one-third of the work, so the project is over, not under.

rw: Intrinsic motivation comes from within, such as enjoying the work itself, so an employee who works hard because she loves the work is intrinsically motivated.

ww.Extrinsic: Extrinsic motivation comes from outside rewards such as pay or praise, but this employee is motivated by enjoyment of the work itself, so it does not describe her.
ww.Coercive: Coercive motivation relies on force or threats, but this employee works hard because she loves the work, so no pressure or threat is involved in her motivation.
ww.Reward-based: Reward-based motivation depends on an outside prize or payment, but she is driven by the work itself and not by anything she receives, so this does not match her reason.

rw: Extrinsic motivation comes from external rewards such as bonuses, pay or praise, so a worker putting in extra hours to earn a bonus is motivated by an outside reward.

ww.Internal: Internal motivation comes from within, like enjoying the work, but this worker is driven by a bonus given by someone else, which is an outside reward.
ww.Social: Social motivation comes from the wish to belong or gain approval from others, but this worker is chasing a money bonus, so the main driver is financial reward.
ww.Intrinsic: Intrinsic motivation comes from personal enjoyment or satisfaction in the task, but this worker is working extra hours for a bonus, which is an external payoff, not an internal one.

rw: Safety needs cover physical security and stability, including a safe workplace and secure employment, so they are the needs met by a safe, stable job.

ww.Physiological: Physiological needs are basic survival needs such as food, water and sleep, and a safe workplace and a stable job address security rather than these bodily needs.
ww.Actualization: Self-actualization is the highest need, about reaching one's full potential, while a safe, stable job relates to security and sits much lower on the hierarchy.
ww.Esteem needs: Esteem needs involve respect, status and recognition from others, but a safe workplace and stable job concern protection and security, so they are not esteem needs.

rw: Esteem needs include recognition, respect and status, so public praise from a manager in front of the team directly addresses this need and makes the employee feel valued.

ww.Safety: Safety needs involve security and stable conditions, such as job stability, and praise does not address safety, so it is not the need being met in this case.
ww.Belonging: Belonging needs are about friendship and acceptance in a group, whereas praise before the team is about recognition and respect, which is the esteem level above belonging.
ww.Physical: Physical needs, also called physiological needs, cover food, water and rest, and praise does not satisfy them, so it is not the need addressed by recognition from a manager.

rw: Salary and working conditions are hygiene factors in Herzberg's theory, because they prevent dissatisfaction but do not by themselves create real motivation, so this is the correct answer.

ww.Achievement and personal growth: Achievement and personal growth are motivators in Herzberg's theory that create satisfaction, not hygiene factors that only prevent dissatisfaction, so they do not answer the question.
ww.Meaningful work and purpose: Meaningful work and purpose relate to the job itself, so they are motivators in Herzberg's theory, and hygiene factors concern the job's surroundings, not its content, so this is not correct.
ww.Recognition from the boss: Recognition is a motivator in Herzberg's theory, because it relates to the work and brings satisfaction, so it is not a hygiene factor, which is related to the job context.

rw: Achievement and recognition are motivators in Herzberg's theory, because they come from the work itself and create real satisfaction and drive, so this is the correct answer.

ww.Company policy and rules: Company policy and rules are hygiene factors, which prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate, so they cannot be the motivators that Herzberg says create real satisfaction.
ww.Salary and annual pay raises: Salary and raises are hygiene factors in Herzberg's theory, which prevent unhappiness but do not create lasting motivation by themselves, so they are not motivators.
ww.Working conditions at work: Working conditions are hygiene factors, since they concern the job's environment rather than the work itself, so they prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate, and they are not motivators.

rw: Expectancy theory says people are motivated when they believe effort leads to performance and that performance leads to rewards they value, so valued rewards complete the chain.

ww.Boredom at work: Boredom is not a result that people expect from performance, and a belief that effort leads to boredom would reduce motivation, so it is not what expectancy theory says.
ww.Punishment: Expecting punishment from good performance would lower motivation, and expectancy theory requires that performance leads to rewards people want, so punishment does not complete the chain.
ww.Nothing at all: If performance led to nothing at all, there would be no reason to try, and motivation would fall, so expectancy theory requires a valued outcome and not an empty result.

rw: Equity theory says people compare their inputs and rewards with those of others, and feeling underpaid compared with a coworker reduces motivation, which matches this situation.

ww.Needs hierarchy: Needs hierarchy explains motivation through levels of human needs, from basic to self-actualization, and not through comparing one's pay with that of a coworker doing the same job.
ww.Scientific theory: Scientific management is about studying tasks to increase efficiency, and it does not explain how comparing one's pay with a coworker's affects motivation, so it is not the theory.
ww.Expectancy theory: Expectancy theory links effort to performance and rewards, but it does not focus on comparing one's pay with others, so it does not explain the feeling of unfairness.

rw: Goal-setting theory says specific, challenging goals with feedback produce the highest performance, because clear targets direct effort and feedback shows progress, so this describes what works best.

ww.Impossible, with no feedback at all: Impossible goals discourage people because they cannot succeed, and having no feedback leaves them with no direction, so this combination lowers motivation instead of raising it.
ww.Vague and easy, with no feedback given: Vague, easy goals give no clear target and little challenge, and with no feedback there is no sense of progress, so this combination does not motivate effectively.
ww.Secret from the team with no feedback gi: Goals kept secret cannot guide the team, and with no feedback members cannot judge progress, so this combination fails to motivate and runs against goal-setting theory.

rw: Autonomy means having control over how and when you do your work, so giving workers a say in organizing their tasks is a way of using autonomy as a motivator.

ww.Oversight: Oversight means close watching and control, which takes freedom away, whereas giving workers a say in how they organize tasks gives them freedom, so it is the opposite of oversight.
ww.Punishment: Punishment uses penalties to force behavior, but letting workers shape how they organize their own tasks is a positive way of motivating, so it is not punishment.
ww.Isolation: Isolation means separating workers from others, and giving workers a say in how they organize tasks is about control over their work, not separating them, so it does not fit.

rw: Theory Y assumes employees enjoy work, are self-motivated and seek responsibility, so managers using it give freedom and trust, and this statement matches the Theory Y view.

ww.Dislike work and need strict control: Disliking work and needing strict control describes Theory X, which is the opposite view, so it does not describe the Theory Y assumptions about employees.
ww.Cannot be trusted with any task: Believing employees cannot be trusted with any task is a negative Theory X type assumption, whereas Theory Y views employees as capable and trustworthy, so this is not correct.
ww.Never want responsibility at all: Believing employees never want responsibility is a Theory X assumption, while Theory Y holds that employees accept and seek responsibility, so this option states the reverse of Theory Y.

rw: Theory X assumes workers dislike work, avoid responsibility and must be closely supervised and controlled, so this statement matches Theory X.

ww.Workers enjoy responsibility and seek ou: Enjoying responsibility and seeking out new tasks is a Theory Y belief, which is the opposite of the Theory X view that workers avoid responsibility.
ww.Workers are self-directed and need littl: Self-directed workers who need little supervision describe a Theory Y belief, but Theory X assumes workers need direction and control, so this statement does not match Theory X.
ww.Workers seek growth and enjoy taking on: Seeking growth and enjoying new duties is a Theory Y belief about motivated workers, which is the opposite of the pessimistic view that defines Theory X.

rw: The Hawthorne studies found that workers' output rose when they received attention and when social factors were considered, showing that human relations influence productivity, so this is the correct finding.

ww.Lighting always lowers output as workers: The Hawthorne studies did not find that lighting always lowers output, because productivity rose even when changes were made to lighting, which points to attention as the cause.
ww.Workers dislike teamwork and work better: The Hawthorne studies highlighted the importance of group relationships and social factors, so they did not show that workers dislike teamwork or work better alone, which reverses the findings.
ww.Pay is the only motivator that matters t: The Hawthorne studies pointed to social factors and attention as motivators, so claiming pay is the only motivator that matters ignores their central finding that other things also matter.

rw: Flexible schedules suit workers with different needs, such as family duties, so they help a company attract and keep employees, which is the main reason to offer one.

ww.To raise product prices for weekend shop: A flexible schedule concerns when employees work, not what customers pay, so it has no direct link to raising product prices for weekend shoppers, and this is not its purpose.
ww.To make work harder for staff on purpose: A flexible schedule gives staff more control over their time, which makes work easier to fit into life, so it does not make work harder on purpose.
ww.To reduce output of the firm for the who: Companies offer flexible schedules to help employees, and reducing output would hurt the firm, so lowering output for the year is not a purpose of flexible scheduling.

rw: A conflict of interest arises when personal ties could influence a business decision, and she did not disclose that the contract went to her brother's company, so this is the ethical issue.

ww.Large cost savings: Cost savings may or may not exist, but the ethical problem is the undisclosed family tie, and awarding the contract to a relative without disclosure is not about savings.
ww.A fair bidding process: A fair bidding process would treat all bidders equally, but favoring her brother's company without disclosing the relationship undermines fairness, so this describes the opposite of the problem.
ww.Good teamwork, as before: Good teamwork has nothing to do with this case, in which she placed a family connection ahead of her duty to the employer, and the concealment is itself the ethical problem.

rw: Declining the gift and reporting it follows company policy, keeps the contract decision fair and protects her integrity, so it is the right response to an expensive gift from a bidder.

ww.Ask for a bigger gift to give the suppli: Asking for a bigger gift is a request for a bribe, which is unethical and likely illegal, so it would make the situation far worse and compromise the buying decision.
ww.Accept it quietly and tell no one about: Accepting the gift quietly and telling no one hides a possible conflict of interest and may violate policy, because secrecy suggests the gift could influence the contract decision.
ww.Give the supplier the contract as a frie: Giving the supplier the contract in return for a gift lets personal benefit decide a business matter, which is corruption, and it ignores fair evaluation of the other bidders.

rw: Notifying customers and recalling the product protects people from harm and shows honesty and responsibility, even though it costs money, so it is the most ethical course of action.

ww.Hide the data from the public and staff: Hiding safety data from the public and staff puts people at risk of injury and is dishonest, and it breaks the duty to protect customers, so it is not ethical.
ww.Keep selling it quietly and say nothing: Continuing to sell a product known to be unsafe, and saying nothing, knowingly exposes customers to harm, which is both unethical and likely illegal, so it is the wrong action.
ww.Blame the customers for the misuse: Blaming customers for misuse avoids responsibility for a defect that is the company's own, and it does nothing to protect people from harm, so it is not an ethical response.

rw: Using the company printer for a personal side business takes company property for private gain without permission, which is misuse of company resources and a breach of workplace ethics.

ww.A donation to the firm's staff: The employee is taking from the firm, not giving, so calling it a donation misdescribes the action, since the firm pays for supplies that benefit only the employee's business.
ww.A normal staff benefit at work: A normal staff benefit is something the employer offers openly, and printing flyers for a side business is not an approved benefit, so describing it that way is incorrect.
ww.A reward for good initiative: Initiative benefits the employer, but printing flyers for a personal side business benefits only the employee, so it deserves no reward and is a misuse of resources.

rw: Asking whether you would be comfortable if everyone saw what you did tests transparency and honesty, because decisions you would hide usually fail ethically, so it is a useful check.

ww.Is it cheaper than the other choices ope: Cost tells you about economics, not about right and wrong, since a cheap option can still be unethical, so asking if it is cheaper does not test whether a decision is ethical.
ww.Will anyone notice if I do this at the o: Asking whether anyone will notice focuses on avoiding detection rather than on right and wrong, so it can lead people to excuse wrongdoing and does not test the decision's ethics.
ww.Is it the easiest option for me to do ri: Choosing the easiest option for yourself puts convenience ahead of what is right, so this question does not check ethics and could encourage a poor decision.

rw: Misrepresentation is giving false or misleading information to gain a sale, and calling a known flawed product perfect is a lie told to the buyer, so this is the correct term.

ww.Fair persuasion: Fair persuasion appeals to buyers honestly and with true information, but telling the buyer a flawed product is perfect is a lie, so it is not fair persuasion.
ww.Honest selling: Honest selling gives truthful information, whereas the salesperson knowingly told the buyer a flawed product was perfect, so the sale is dishonest and not an example of honest selling.
ww.Fair negotiating: Fair negotiating involves honest exchange of offers, and a salesperson who lies about a known flaw is not negotiating fairly, so this does not describe the situation.

rw: Promoting a friend over a better qualified employee treats people unequally and goes against fairness, which requires that decisions be based on merit and not on personal ties.

ww.Profit: Profit is a business goal and is not the principle at risk when a friend is promoted over a better qualified person, since the issue is how people are treated.
ww.Efficiency: Efficiency is about using resources well, and while a poor promotion may lower efficiency, the main principle at risk is fairness to the more qualified employee, not efficiency.
ww.Speed: Speed concerns how fast something is done and has no bearing on favoritism in promotions, since the issue is whether the decision is fair to the better qualified employee.

rw: Ethical relativism holds that right and wrong depend on cultural or personal standards instead of being universal, so this statement defines the term correctly.

ww.The belief in one set of rules everywher: Believing in one set of rules everywhere is ethical absolutism or universalism, which is the opposite of relativism, which holds that standards vary with culture and persons.
ww.The belief that ethics do not exist at a: Ethical relativism does not deny that ethics exist, but holds that moral standards differ across cultures or individuals, so saying ethics do not exist misstates the view.
ww.The belief that only laws matter in busi: Relativism does not claim that only laws matter, because it says moral standards come from culture or personal views, so equating ethics with law alone is a different position.

rw: Deontological ethics judges actions by whether they follow moral duties or rules, regardless of the results, so an action is right if it respects those duties.

ww.Judging actions only by their results an: Judging actions only by their results is consequentialism, such as utilitarianism, which is the opposite of deontology, which looks at duty and rules instead of outcomes.
ww.Doing what is popular with most people i: Doing what is popular is following social opinion, and deontology looks to moral duties and rules, which may differ from what most people prefer, so this is not the right definition.
ww.Doing what is legal only, with no though: Doing only what is legal ignores moral duties that go beyond the law, whereas deontology concerns moral rules and duty, so it is not the same as legal compliance.

rw: Utilitarianism judges actions by their consequences and favors the action that produces the greatest good for the greatest number of people, which is exactly what this statement says.

ww.Following rules regardless of results, s: Following rules regardless of results is deontology, which looks at duty and not consequences, so it is the opposite of utilitarianism, which weighs outcomes.
ww.Doing what is traditional in a culture,: Doing what is traditional in a culture is following custom, which is a different idea from utilitarianism, which judges by outcomes for the greatest number rather than by tradition.
ww.Doing what a leader says, whatever the r: Obeying a leader whatever the results is obedience to authority, whereas utilitarianism weighs the effects of an action on everyone, so it does not match the definition.

rw: Dumping waste in a river harms the environment and the community, and a company owes responsibility to society and nature, so it violates social and environmental responsibility.

ww.Profit maximization, since the firm save: Profit maximization is a business aim, and dumping waste to save money serves profit but harms others, so it is not a principle that the action violates.
ww.Cost control of waste in the plant: Cost control is a legitimate goal, but saving money by polluting a river harms others, so cost control is not the principle violated and the harm is an ethical issue.
ww.Good management of the firm's costs: Good management of costs is generally a positive practice, but dumping waste in a river to save money is harmful, so this is not the principle being violated.

rw: Data is facts, numbers or observations that can be recorded and later analyzed, so this statement gives the standard definition of data in data science.

ww.Software that carries out instructions o: Software is a set of programs that carry out instructions, which is a different thing from data, which is the information that software stores and processes.
ww.Machines that store information inside a: Machines that store information are hardware such as servers or drives, which hold data but are not the data itself, so this describes equipment and not data.
ww.Opinions that nobody has written down an: Opinions that nobody has written down are not recorded information, but data must be something recorded, so an unrecorded opinion does not fit the definition.

rw: The number of customers who visited today is a count, which is numeric and measurable, so it is quantitative data, which can be used in calculations and statistics.

ww.A customer's description of the store's: A description of the atmosphere is made of words about qualities and impressions, not numbers, so it is qualitative data and not quantitative data.
ww.A customer's favorite flavor of ice crea: A favorite flavor is a category described in words and not a measured number, so it is qualitative data, not quantitative.
ww.The color of a store's front door and it: The color of a door is a descriptive quality rather than a measurement, so it is qualitative data, which does not use numbers.

rw: Written comments from a survey describe opinions and experiences in words rather than numbers, so they are qualitative data, which captures qualities and impressions.

ww.The price of an item in dollars each ove: The price of an item in dollars is a number that can be measured and used in calculations, so it is quantitative data and not qualitative.
ww.The weight of a package in kilograms: The weight of a package in kilograms is a measured number, which is quantitative data, and not a description of qualities, so it is not qualitative.
ww.The number of items sold in a week: The number of items sold in a week is a count, which is numeric and measurable, so it is quantitative data and not qualitative.

rw: Structured data fits into tables with defined fields, such as rows and columns, whereas unstructured data, such as emails or images, has no such fixed format, which is the difference.

ww.Structured data is only text while unstr: Both types can contain text or numbers, so structured data is not only text and unstructured data is not only numbers, and this statement reverses nothing useful about how they are organized.
ww.Structured data is always larger than un: Size does not distinguish the two types, since unstructured data like video files can be far larger than structured tables, so structured data is not always larger.
ww.Structured data is stored on paper while: The difference concerns the organization of the data and not the storage medium, because both types are stored digitally, and saying structured data is on paper is incorrect.

rw: Names, dates and order totals in labeled columns follow a fixed, organized format of rows and columns, which is what structured data means, so this example is structured data.

ww.A computer network: A computer network is a group of connected computers that share resources, which is a type of system and is not a way of organizing data in rows and columns.
ww.Unstructured data: Unstructured data has no fixed format, such as free text, images or audio, but a spreadsheet with labeled columns follows a clear structure, so it is not unstructured.
ww.A neural network: A neural network is a machine learning model made of connected nodes, which is not a data layout, and a spreadsheet with labeled columns is not a neural network.

rw: A data source is the place or system where data originates or is obtained, such as a database, sensor or survey, so this statement defines the term correctly.

ww.The person who reads the final report: The person who reads the final report is the audience or user of the results, and is not the origin of the data, so this does not define a data source.
ww.The rule that decides how data is stored: A rule deciding how data is stored is a data standard or policy, which governs structure, but it is not where the data comes from, so it is not a source.
ww.The final chart that presents the findin: A final chart that presents the findings is an output of analysis and comes at the end of the process, so it is the result and not the source of data.

rw: Primary data is collected firsthand by the researcher for a specific purpose, such as through surveys or experiments, so this statement defines primary data correctly.

ww.Data that is stored in a cloud service f: Storing data in a cloud service describes where it is kept and not how it was collected, so it does not define primary data, which is classified by who gathered it.
ww.Data copied from a report that someone e: Data copied from a report that someone else wrote is collected by another person earlier, which is secondary data, so it is the opposite of primary data.
ww.Data that is always numeric and exact to: Primary data can be text or categories as well as numbers, and exactness has nothing to do with whether it was collected firsthand, so this is not a definition.

rw: Secondary data was collected earlier by someone else for another purpose and is reused, such as government statistics or published reports, so this statement defines it correctly.

ww.Data that is stored in a backup file for: Storing data in a backup file describes how it is kept, not who collected it, so this statement does not define secondary data, which is classified by its origin.
ww.Data that is less important than other d: Secondary data is not necessarily less important, and it can be very valuable, because the term refers to who collected it, not how important it is to the study.
ww.Data you collect yourself for the first: Data that you collect yourself for the first time is primary data, which is the opposite of secondary data collected earlier by someone else, so this is the wrong definition.

rw: Data quality describes how accurate, complete and consistent the data is, which determines whether the data can be trusted for decisions, so this is the right definition.

ww.How much storage the data uses on the se: Storage use describes the size of the data and not its quality, because a file can be large and still inaccurate, so this is not what data quality means.
ww.How colorful and attractive a chart of t: How a chart looks concerns visual presentation and not the data itself, and an attractive chart can still show poor data, so appearance is not data quality.
ww.How fast the data can be copied or sent: Speed of copying or sending data concerns performance and transfer, not whether the data is accurate or complete, so it is unrelated to data quality.

rw: Many missing or incorrect values reduce accuracy and completeness, so conclusions drawn from the data may be wrong, which makes the data set unreliable.

ww.Clear column names and labels: Clear column names and labels make data easier to understand and use, so they improve reliability instead of causing a problem, and they do not make a data set unreliable.
ww.Documentation of the data source: Documenting where data comes from helps users judge its trustworthiness, so it supports reliability and does not make a data set unreliable.
ww.A consistent date format used: A consistent date format makes records comparable and easy to process, so it helps reliability and is a strength and not a problem that makes a data set unreliable.

rw: Data cleaning means finding and fixing errors, gaps and duplicates so that the data is accurate and usable, which is the standard definition of the process.

ww.Printing the data on clean paper for the: Printing data on clean paper is only a physical presentation and does nothing to correct problems in the data, so it is not what data cleaning means.
ww.Making charts look more attractive to th: Making charts look attractive is visualization or design work, which comes after analysis, and does not correct errors in the data, so it is not data cleaning.
ww.Deleting all the data to start again fro: Deleting all the data destroys the information and forces a restart, whereas cleaning fixes specific problems and keeps the valid data, so it is not the meaning of cleaning.

rw: A duplicate record counts the same customer twice and can distort totals and counts, so removing the extra copy keeps the data accurate, which is the correct action.

ww.Change the customer's name: Changing the customer's name would alter correct information and create an error, and it does not solve the problem of the repeated entry, so it is the wrong fix.
ww.Delete the whole data table: Deleting the whole table would destroy all the other valid records for a small issue, so it is an extreme and harmful response to one repeated entry.
ww.Keep both records to be safe: Keeping both records leaves the customer double counted, which distorts totals and analysis, so keeping duplicates to be safe leaves the data quality problem unsolved.

rw: An age of 250 is not plausible, so the analyst should check whether it is an entry error and then correct or remove it, which protects the data quality.

ww.Replace every other age in the column wi: Replacing every other age with 250 would corrupt the whole column with false values, making the data far worse and spreading one error across all the records.
ww.Leave it as it is because all the data i: Assuming all data is valid ignores an obvious impossible value, and leaving 250 in place would distort the results, so this fails to protect the quality of the data.
ww.Use it to compute the average without ch: Using the value in the average without checking would pull the average upward with a false number, so the results would be wrong, and the value must be checked first.

rw: A missing value is an entry where no data was recorded, leaving a blank in the data set, which is the standard meaning of the term in data work.

ww.A value that has been rounded off: A rounded value still has data recorded, only with fewer decimal places, so it is not missing, because a missing value is one where nothing was recorded.
ww.A value that is repeated many times: A value repeated many times is a frequent value, and the number is recorded each time, so it is not missing, because missing means no data was entered.
ww.A value that is the largest one: The largest value in a set is the maximum, and it is recorded, so it is not missing, because a missing value has no entry at all.

rw: An outlier is a value that lies far from the rest of the data, such as an extremely high or low number, and it can distort statistics, so this is the correct definition.

ww.A value that appears most often in a set: The value that appears most often is the mode, which describes a typical value, so it is the opposite of an outlier, which is unusual.
ww.A value that is exactly in the middle: The value exactly in the middle is the median, a measure of the center, so it describes a central value and not an unusual one, as an outlier does.
ww.A value that equals the average value: A value equal to the average is the mean, which is typical of the data, so it is not an outlier, because an outlier lies far from the others.

rw: A data dictionary explains what each field means and how it is recorded, such as formats and units, so users interpret the data correctly, which is why it is used.

ww.It increases the size of the data on pur: A data dictionary does not add size to the data, because it is a separate description document, and enlarging the data on purpose would serve no useful goal.
ww.It deletes fields that no one uses from: A data dictionary describes fields and does not delete anything, since removing unused fields would be a separate cleanup task and not the purpose of documentation.
ww.It replaces the need for any column name: A data dictionary does not replace column names, because it explains them, so tables still need names, and documentation supports the names instead of removing the need for them.

rw: A database is an organized collection of data stored so that it can be searched, retrieved and updated efficiently, so this statement gives the standard definition.

ww.A program that edits photographs and oth: A program that edits photographs is image editing software, which is a different tool, and a database is a system for storing data, not a program for changing pictures.
ww.A single chart showing sales over time,: A single chart updated monthly is a report or visualization of data, and a database is a stored collection of data that supports many such outputs, so it is not the same thing.
ww.A device that connects to the internet t: A device that connects to the internet by wireless link describes a router or access point, which is hardware for networking, and does not describe a database.

rw: A primary key is a field whose value is unique for each record, so every row can be identified exactly, which is the standard definition of a primary key.

ww.A field that is always left blank in eac: A field that is always blank would not identify anything, whereas a primary key must contain a value in every row, so it fails the main requirement of a key.
ww.A field that stores user passwords safel: Passwords are sensitive data stored with security measures, and a primary key is not about storing passwords but about identifying records, so this does not describe it.
ww.A field that repeats in every row with o: A field that repeats a single value in every row cannot tell records apart, so it fails the uniqueness requirement and cannot serve as a primary key.

rw: A unique customer ID number is different for each customer, never repeats and stays stable, so it identifies each record exactly and is the best choice for a primary key.

ww.The customer's first name: Many customers share a first name, so it is not unique, and a primary key must be different for every record, which means a first name would fail as one.
ww.The customer's home city: Many customers live in the same city, so the home city is not unique and cannot identify a single record, which means it is a poor choice for a key.
ww.The customer's favorite color: Many customers share a favorite color, so it is not unique and could change, which means it cannot identify each record and does not work as a primary key.

rw: Big data means data sets so large, fast or varied that ordinary tools cannot handle them, so special tools are needed, which is the standard definition.

ww.Data that comes only from large companie: Big data is defined by size, speed and variety, not by the type of company that produces it, so limiting it to large companies and banks is incorrect.
ww.Any file larger than one megabyte in siz: A file of one megabyte is small by modern standards, so size alone does not make data big, and big data refers to volumes needing special tools to handle.
ww.Data printed in large letters on posters: Printing data in large letters on posters concerns display and has nothing to do with big data, which is defined by the volume, speed and variety of data.

rw: The three Vs of big data are volume, which is the amount, velocity, which is the speed of arrival, and variety, which is the range of types, so this is correct.

ww.Visual, verbal and vocal: Visual, verbal and vocal are descriptions of communication styles and not features of big data, so this is not the correct set of three Vs for big data.
ww.Vendor, version and validity: Vendor, version and validity are not the standard three Vs of big data, which concern the volume, speed and variety of the data, so this set is wrong.
ww.Value, vision and voice only: Value, vision and voice are not the standard three Vs, because the established list is volume, velocity and variety, so this set is not the accepted one.

rw: A data set is a collection of related data, often arranged in a table of rows and columns, so this statement defines a data set correctly.

ww.A rule that decides who may view all the: A rule deciding who may view data files is an access control policy, which governs permissions and does not define a data set, which is the collection of data itself.
ww.A tool that draws charts from the number: A tool that draws charts is visualization software, which uses data but is not the data, so it describes a tool and not a data set.
ww.A device that records sound in a recordi: A device that records sound is audio equipment, which can produce data, but a data set is a collection of data and not a recording device.

rw: Consistent data uses the same formats, units and conventions across all records, so values can be compared and combined reliably, which is what consistency means.

ww.It is stored in a secret location on a s: Storing data in a secret location concerns security and has nothing to do with whether the values are uniform, so it does not define consistency.
ww.It contains only whole numbers and no de: Consistent data does not need to contain only whole numbers, because decimals are acceptable if they are used uniformly, so this is not what consistency means.
ww.It has never been changed by anyone sinc: Data that has never been changed may still be inconsistent or wrong, and legitimate updates are normal, so unchanged data is not the same as consistent data.

rw: Prices in two currencies with no labels mix dollars and euros so the numbers cannot be compared, which is a problem of inconsistent units, and this answer names it.

ww.A duplicate record: A duplicate record is the same entry appearing twice, but here the problem is that the values are measured in different currencies without labels, so it is not duplication.
ww.An outlier value: An outlier is a value far from the rest of the data, but the problem here is mixed currencies, which affect many values and not a single unusual one.
ww.A missing value: A missing value is an entry with no data recorded, but both columns hold prices, so the problem is that the units differ and are unlabeled, not that data is absent.
